analysis.one_liner: Creates a national paid family and medical leave program funded by a 0.2% payroll tax on workers and employers.
analysis.headline: The FAMILY Act, a national paid leave bill with 160 House cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote and died in committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give workers up to 60 days of paid leave per year to care for a new child, a seriously ill family member, or their own serious health condition. Benefits would be paid monthly — between $580 and $4,000, scaled to past earnings — through a new office in the Social Security Administration. It would be financed by a 0.2% payroll tax on both employees and employers, plus 0.4% on self-employment income. It also made it illegal to fire or penalize a worker for using the benefit.
analysis.who_benefits: Working people who today have no access to paid leave. The bill's own findings state that only 14% of U.S. workers had employer-provided paid family leave, and it was available to just 4% of people in the lowest-paying jobs [S3]. Nearly half of workers who qualified for unpaid leave under the 1993 FMLA law took none of it because they could not afford to go without a paycheck [S3]. The new program would cover everyone with recent earnings, including the self-employed and railroad workers, with a minimum monthly benefit of $580 so low earners get meaningful replacement [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Provides up to 60 paid caregiving days per year, with monthly benefits between $580 and $4,000 based on prior earnings, administered by the Social Security Administration.
Funded by a 0.2% tax each on employee wages and employer payrolls and 0.4% on self-employment income, paid into a dedicated trust fund — not taken from Social Security's own trust funds.
Makes it unlawful to fire or discriminate against a worker for applying for or using the benefit, with damages and reinstatement available in court.
Covers caring for a domestic partner and their children, and coordinates with state paid-leave programs rather than replacing them.

analysis.who_pays: Every employer and every worker with wages pays the new 0.2% payroll tax; self-employed people pay 0.4% of self-employment income. Employers also face civil liability if they retaliate against workers who use the benefit. For a worker making $50,000, the employee share is about $100 a year.

drawbacks.text: The bill adds a new payroll tax on every worker and employer, on top of existing Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes — a real cost, though small (0.2% of wages).
Benefits are capped at 60 days and the monthly amount is a fraction of wages for higher earners, so it would not fully replace income for longer absences.
Employers bear new legal liability, including damages and attorney's fees, when workers claim they were penalized for taking leave, which small businesses would have to manage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is small and broad: a 0.2% payroll tax on everyone in exchange for paid leave that today only 14% of workers have through their employers, and that reaches only 4% of the lowest-paid jobs. The costs are real but modest and spread widely; the benefits are large for the workers who currently face a choice between caring for a newborn or sick relative and losing their income or job. Design flaws exist — the 60-day cap and the benefit formula limit coverage — but the bill sets up a functioning insurance pool rather than an unfunded mandate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Ways and Means Committee, was passed down to its Human Resources subcommittee, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 7, 2017 by Rep. Rosa DeLauro and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
Two weeks later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Human Resources, where it stayed; no further action was taken for the rest of the 115th Congress.
The bill accumulated 160 cosponsors, all of them House Democrats.
The committee that controlled the bill never scheduled a markup or hearing, and the bill never reached the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have paid the new 0.2% payroll tax, and the status quo generally: workers without access to paid leave remain without it, and the bill's cosponsors gained no policy outcome. Supporters re-introduced the same concept in later Congresses.

sides.party_line_note: All 160 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsor appears in the record, and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would impose a 0.2% payroll tax on every employer and create legal liability for firing or penalizing workers who use paid leave. Employer groups preferred the status quo, where only 14% of workers have employer-paid family leave.

A federal paid-leave benefit administered by the Social Security Administration would substitute for the short-term disability insurance that fewer than 40% of workers get through employers today, reducing that private market over time.

industries.industry: Low-wage service workers and their families
industries.note: Paid family leave was available to just 4% of workers in the lowest-paying jobs; the bill's minimum monthly benefit of $580 was designed so low earners receive meaningful wage replacement.
